subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: At the community centre's Saturday story hour, Gautam sat between his five-year-old twins. Ojas had already told the librarian about his loose tooth, the dog next door and a dream about trains. Ila sat pressed against his arm, silent, turning pages. "Say hi to the other kids, Ila," Gautam whispered. Ila shrank. Ojas tugged his other sleeve. "Papa, listen, listen!" Gautam felt split down the middle. Then he stopped pushing. He let Ojas sit in the front row and stayed at the back with Ila, reading quietly. On the way out, Ila whispered the whole story back to him.

qa.q: What did Ojas tell the librarian about?
qa.a: His loose tooth, the dog next door and a dream about trains.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel with one twin tugging and the other pressed against him?
qa.a: He felt split down the middle, pulled between Ojas's chatter and Ila's quiet.

qa.q: What turning point came when Gautam stopped pushing Ila to say hi?
qa.a: He gave each twin the attention they needed, Ojas in the front row and Ila reading quietly, and Ila later whispered the whole story back.

qa.q: How might Ila have felt when told to say hi to the other kids?
qa.a: She shrank, so she likely felt pressured and uncomfortable at being pushed to act like her brother.

grounding: A father of a chatty twin and a quiet twin feels torn, then gives each child the kind of attention they need.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: From my balcony across the lane, I, Jahnavi, see Vasudha's evenings. Her son Rudra, six, talks from the moment the school van drops him. Her daughter Pari, four, goes under the dining table with her crayons and stays silent. Last week Vasudha said, "Pari, come out and talk like your brother." Pari cried, and Rudra went quiet too. Vasudha rubbed her forehead; I can't say what she was thinking. The next evening she sat on the step letting Rudra chatter, then carried a cup of milk under the table and sat silently with Pari. Both children looked easy again.

qa.q: Where does Pari go with her crayons?
qa.a: She goes under the dining table.

qa.q: What might Vasudha rubbing her forehead suggest, given Jahnavi can't be sure?
qa.a: It suggests she may have felt tired or torn, pulled between one child's chatter and the other's silence.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make the next evening, and what came of it?
qa.a: She gave each child a different kind of time, chatter with Rudra and silence with Pari, and both looked easy again.

qa.q: Why might Rudra have gone quiet when Pari was told to talk like him?
qa.a: He may have felt he had done something wrong, since being held up as the example had upset his sister.

grounding: A neighbour watches a mother of a talkative son and a quiet daughter learn that forcing sameness hurts both children.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Ramesh sat on a tiny chair between his two children. Kamal, six, had already told Ms. Pinto about the lizard in the bathroom and his new shoes. Chhavi, five, held Ramesh's sleeve and said nothing. 'Chhavi is bright,' said Ms. Pinto, 'but she must speak up like her brother.' Ramesh felt the familiar pull. At home Kamal chattered till bedtime; Chhavi needed quiet mornings with her drawings. 'She talks,' he said. 'Just not in a crowd. Yesterday she told me a whole story, alone with me. I don't want her made into Kamal.' Chhavi's grip loosened.

qa.q: What did Kamal tell Ms. Pinto about?
qa.a: The lizard in the bathroom and his new shoes.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when Ms. Pinto compared the children?
qa.a: He felt the familiar pull between them, uneasy and protective, not wanting Chhavi pushed to be like Kamal.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's reply get right?
qa.a: It explained that Chhavi talks in her own way, alone and quietly, and refused to force her to match her brother.

qa.q: How might Chhavi feel when her grip loosens?
qa.a: Chhavi probably feels relieved and safe, understood by Ramesh instead of pushed.

grounding: Shows a parent pulled between a chatty child and a quiet one, who refuses to force them into sameness.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. At a loud birthday party Uma pushed both children onto the dance floor. Nakul whooped; Pooja, five, hid behind the curtain and cried.
Wednesday. Worn out by Nakul's chatter, Uma declared quiet time for both. Nakul, four, kicked the sofa and wailed. Pooja finally smiled.
Saturday. Uma sent Nakul to the park with the neighbour's boys and sat alone with Pooja, rolling dough in silence. When Nakul burst back full of stories, she listened to every one. That night she felt tired, but less torn.

qa.q: Where did Pooja hide at the party?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: How did Uma feel on Saturday night, and why?
qa.a: She felt tired but less torn, because each child had got the kind of attention they needed.

qa.q: What did Uma learn from Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Forcing both children into the same thing upset one of them each time; giving each a different kind of time worked better.

qa.q: What was Wednesday's quiet time like for Nakul?
qa.a: Nakul felt frustrated and trapped, kicking the sofa and wailing, because quiet suits Pooja, not him.

grounding: Shows a parent of a lively child and a quiet child learning that forcing the same activity hurts both, and that each needs different attention.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: The power went out at seven, and the whole flat shrank to one candlelit room. Suraj, six, talked without stopping: shadows, lizards, what if the lights never came back. Mira, four, pressed her hands over her ears and began to whimper. Urmila felt pulled in two. 'Suraj, shush!' she snapped, and his face crumpled. She took a breath. Then she gave Mira the torch and the quiet corner with her picture book, and took Suraj to the doorway to make shadow animals, whispering. Soon Mira was turning pages, and Suraj was giggling at a shadow crocodile.

qa.q: What did Urmila give Mira?
qa.a: The torch and the quiet corner with her picture book.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when both children needed her at once?
qa.a: She felt pulled in two and snapped, then stopped to calm herself.

qa.q: What worked better than 'Suraj, shush'?
qa.a: Giving each child a different kind of attention: quiet space for Mira and whispered shadow play with Suraj.

qa.q: What was it like for Suraj when Urmila snapped?
qa.a: Suraj felt hurt and his face crumpled; his chatter was how he coped with the dark.

grounding: Shows a parent pulled between a chatty child and a quiet one during a power cut, who finds a different kind of attention for each.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: At the Lucknow Sunday market, Ojas, five, chatted to every vendor about mangoes, dogs and his new tooth. His twin, Mitali, held her father's finger and stared at her sandals. "Say hello to Uncle, Mitali," Uday urged. She shrank behind him. Uday felt pulled two ways and a little frustrated. Then he remembered her silence after last week's party. He let Ojas chat with the banana seller and walked Mitali to the quiet end of the market, where she silently pointed out three pigeons and a cat. Riding home, Ojas talked nonstop; Mitali leaned on her father, content.

qa.q: What did Ojas chat to vendors about?
qa.a: Mangoes, dogs and his new tooth.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Mitali shrank behind him?
qa.a: He felt pulled two ways and a little frustrated, trying to meet both children's needs at once.

qa.q: What did Uday do that respected both children?
qa.a: He let Ojas chat with the banana seller and took Mitali to a quiet spot, giving each a different kind of attention.

qa.q: How might Mitali feel leaning on her father on the way home?
qa.a: Mitali may feel safe and content, understood without being pushed to talk.

grounding: Shows a parent of a chatty child and a quiet child, feeling pulled between them, giving each a different kind of attention instead of forcing sameness.
